title: Homomorphisms and maps from cyclic groups
section: Part B: Abstract Algebra ▷ Group Homomorphisms
terms: group homomorphism; monomorphism; epimorphism; endomorphism; automorphism; homomorphic image.

exposition.text:
A homomorphism preserves multiplication, hence the identity and inverses. A monomorphism
is injective, an epimorphism is surjective for groups, an endomorphism has the same domain
and codomain, and an automorphism is a bijective endomorphism. Images and inverse images
of subgroups under a homomorphism are subgroups.
The order of f (g) divides the finite order of g; equality is guaranteed when f is injective, not
for arbitrary homomorphisms. A map from Z is determined by the image of 1, which must

question.text:
How many group homomorphisms are there from Z to Z ?
18 30
(A) 3 (B) 5 (C) 6 (D) 9 (E) 15

solution.text:
The image y of 1 must satisfy 18y = 0 (mod 30). This congruence has gcd(18, 30) = 6 solu-
tions, each defining exactly one homomorphism.

question.text:
How many surjective homomorphisms Z → Z are there?
24 8
(A) 2 (B) 4 (C) 6 (D) 8 (E) 12

solution.text:
The image of 1 must generate Z , hence be 1, 3, 5, or 7. Each works because 8 | 24, so the
8
relation 24 · 1 = 0 is respected. There are four maps.

question.text:
Which formula defines a group homomorphism f : Z → Z ?
6 4
(A) f ([x] ) = [x] (B) f([x] ) = [2x]
6 4 6 4
2
(C) f([x] ) = [x + 1] (D) f([x] ) = [x ]
6 4 6 4
(E) f([x] ) = [3x]
6 4

solution.text:
The image of the generator must be killed by six modulo four, which holds for the image
two. Equivalently replacing x by x + 6 changes 2x by twelve, a multiple of four, and addi-
tivity holds. A and E depend on the representative; C also fails the identity condition; D is
well defined but fails additivity at 1 + 1.

question.text:
Compare the endomorphisms f : Z → Z and g : Q → Q, both given by multiplication by two.
Which statement is correct?
(A) Both are automorphisms.
(B) f is a monomorphism but not an epimorphism, while g is an automorphism.
(C) f is an epimorphism but not a monomorphism, while g is an automorphism.
(D) Neither is injective.
(E) Neither is a homomorphism.

solution.text:
Multiplication by two is additive and injective in both groups. In Z its image omits odd
integers, whereas every rational q is the image of q/2. Thus the same algebraic rule has
different surjectivity depending on the group.

question.text:
Finite groups G, H have orders twenty-seven and twenty, respectively. How many group homo-
morphisms G → H exist?
(A) 0 (B) 1 (C) 3 (D) 9 (E) 20

solution.text:
For any g ∈ G, its order divides twenty-seven, and the order of its image divides that
order as well as twenty. The only common divisor is one, so every element maps to the
identity. The trivial map exists, giving exactly one homomorphism, without any cyclicity
assumption on G.

Let f : Z → Z be f(a, b) = 3a + 4b (mod 12), and let H = {0, 6}. What is f (H)?
12
(A) 2Z × 3Z (B) 3Z × 2Z (C) 6Z × Z (D) Z × 6Z (E) {(a, b) : a + b ≡ 0 (mod 6)}

solution.text:
Belonging to H means 3a + 4b is divisible by six. Modulo two this forces a even, and modulo
three it forces b divisible by three. Conversely these two conditions make the expression
divisible by six. Thus the inverse image is the displayed subgroup of the domain.

For a group G, the inversion map j(g) = g is a bijection. When is it a group endomorphism?
(A) For every group
(B) Exactly when G is finite
(C) Exactly when G is cyclic
(D) Exactly when G is Abelian
(E) Only for the trivial group

solution.text:
−1 −1 −1 −1
Always j(ab) = b a , while j(a)j(b) = a b . These are equal for all a, b exactly when
all inverse elements commute, equivalently when G is Abelian. Bijection by itself does not
make a map an automorphism.
